name: Wireless & Cellular Security
description: Security of cellular (4G/5G), Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, and other RF/wireless protocols.

ccs.narrative:
Research on wireless and cellular security at CCS began taking shape around 2018, with early work concentrating on wireless protocol security, cellular attacks, and RF-based threats. A Formal Analysis of 5G Authentication (CCS 2018) set an influential baseline by showing how to Formally analyzes the 5G authenticated key exchange protocol, identifying security guarantees and gaps. Parallel contributions—5GReasoner: A Property-Directed Security and Privacy Analysis Framework for 5G Cellular Network Protocol (2019) and Screaming Channels: When Electromagnetic Side Channels Meet Radio Transceivers (2018) —reinforced the foundational challenges in this space.

A productive wave of CCS work from 2020–2022 deepened the area. Robust Adversarial Attacks Against DNN-Based Wireless Communication Systems (CCS 2021) advanced the field by demonstrating Crafts robust adversarial perturbations against DNN-based channel estimation and decoding in OFDM wireless systems. Other strong contributions included FirmXRay: Detecting Bluetooth Link Layer Vulnerabilities From Bare-Metal Firmware (2020), Noncompliance as Deviant Behavior: An Automated Black-box Noncompliance Checker for 4G LTE Cellular Devices (2021), broadening the space of techniques and targets.

The most recent CCS contributions (from 2023 onward) reflect a maturing field that pushes into harder targets and broader threat models. Password-Stealing without Hacking: Wi-Fi Enabled Practical Keystroke Eavesdropping (CCS 2023) exemplified this trend by tackling Eavesdrops keystrokes via commodity Wi-Fi signals without hacking hardware, stealing passwords. Similarly, Watch This Space: Securing Satellite Communication through Resilient Transmitter Fingerprinting (2023) and Formal Analysis of Access Control Mechanism of 5G Core Network (2023) show how the community continues to scale and adapt its methods.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list zero in on two themes that would recur for years: spoofing of physical-layer signals and the messy security of legacy interfaces. "All Your GPS Are Belong To Us: Towards Stealthy Manipulation of Road Navigation Systems" (USENIX 2018) showed that GPS spoofing could be made stealthy enough to quietly reroute drivers, while "ATtention Spanned: Comprehensive Vulnerability Analysis of AT Commands Within the Android Ecosystem" (USENIX 2018) revealed that 1980s-era modem commands still expose modern smartphones, and "Off-Path TCP Exploit: How Wireless Routers Can Jeopardize Your Secrets" (USENIX 2018) turned a Wi-Fi half-duplex timing side channel into a remote secret-stealing attack. Together they framed wireless security as a problem of trusting open mediums and inherited legacy protocols.

By 2019-2020 the field pivoted hard toward the cellular and short-range stacks. On LTE, "Hiding in Plain Signal: Physical Signal Overshadowing Attack on LTE" (USENIX 2019) demonstrated that an attacker could overshadow legitimate broadcasts, and "Call Me Maybe: Eavesdropping Encrypted LTE Calls With ReVoLTE" (USENIX 2020) broke voice confidentiality by exploiting keystream reuse. Bluetooth saw a parallel wave: "The KNOB is Broken: Exploiting Low Entropy in the Encryption Key Negotiation Of Bluetooth BR/EDR" (USENIX 2019) attacked the standard itself, while "Frankenstein: Advanced Wireless Fuzzing to Exploit New Bluetooth Escalation Targets" (USENIX 2020) brought systematic fuzzing to firmware. The period also broadened the attack surface to proprietary and vehicular wireless links, from "A Billion Open Interfaces for Eve and Mallory" (USENIX 2019) on Apple Wireless Direct Link to "Plug-N-Pwned" (USENIX 2020) on automotive OBD-II dongles.

From 2021 onward the work matured from one-off exploits toward privacy attacks, defenses, and automated, specification-grounded analysis. Side channels grew subtler, with "A Stealthy Location Identification Attack Exploiting Carrier Aggregation in Cellular Networks" (USENIX 2021) and "Watching the Watchers: Practical Video Identification Attack in LTE Networks" (USENIX 2022) inferring location and even streamed video from encrypted traffic. Defenders answered with practical countermeasures like "Stars Can Tell: A Robust Method to Defend against GPS Spoofing Attacks using Off-the-shelf Chipset" (USENIX 2021) and protocol fixes such as "Privacy-Preserving and Standard-Compatible AKA Protocol for 5G" (USENIX 2021) and "Formal Analysis and Patching of BLE-SC Pairing" (USENIX 2023).

The most recent thread is scale: rather than hunting bugs by hand, researchers now reason over standards and baseband implementations automatically. "DoLTEst" (USENIX 2022) systematized negative testing of LTE devices, "Seeing the Forest for the Trees" (USENIX 2022) mined 3GPP change requests for spec-level hazards, "Sherlock on Specs" (USENIX 2023) and "BASECOMP" (USENIX 2023) tackled conformance testing and baseband integrity, and "Logic Gone Astray: A Security Analysis Framework for the Control Plane Protocols of 5G Basebands" (USENIX 2024) brought differential testing to 5G control-plane logic. The arc runs from clever physical-layer spoofs to automated, formal scrutiny of the cellular ecosystem itself.

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list mark wireless security's pivot from informal probing to rigorous, systematic scrutiny of cellular standards. On the formal side, "A Formal Analysis of 5G Authentication" (CCS 2018) used symbolic model checking to expose weaknesses in the 5G AKA protocol even before deployment, while "LTEInspector" (NDSS 2018) paired a model checker with a real testbed to uncover practical attacks on 4G attach, detach, and paging. In parallel, hands-on work showed these protocols were exploitable in the field: "Breaking LTE on Layer Two" (S&P 2019) revealed that LTE's unauthenticated layer-two could be manipulated to redirect and fingerprint traffic, and "Hiding in Plain Signal" (USENIX 2019) demonstrated overshadowing a legitimate LTE signal over the air. Beyond cellular, this period also surfaced the broader RF attack surface: "All Your GPS Are Belong To Us" (USENIX 2018) showed stealthy road-navigation spoofing, and "Screaming Channels" (CCS 2018) found that electromagnetic side channels can leak secrets straight through the radios of Bluetooth and Wi-Fi chips.

A clear shift followed: formal analysis and dynamic testing became the dominant methodology, fanning out across venues. "5GReasoner" (CCS 2019) and "Component-Based Formal Analysis of 5G-AKA" (NDSS 2019) extended property-directed verification deeper into the 5G stack, while "Touching the Untouchables" (S&P 2019) built dynamic testing of the LTE control plane. Privacy emerged as its own thread, with "GUTI Reallocation Demystified" (NDSS 2018) and "Privacy Attacks to the 4G and 5G Cellular Paging Protocols" (NDSS 2019) turning temporary identifiers and paging side channels into location-tracking attacks. The short-range wireless world saw the same maturation: "The KNOB is Broken" (USENIX 2019) and "BIAS" (S&P 2020) broke Bluetooth's key negotiation and impersonation guarantees, "Dragonblood" (S&P 2020) cracked the WPA3 handshake, and "Frankenstein" (USENIX 2020) brought advanced fuzzing to Bluetooth firmware.

By the early 2020s the field broadened in two directions: down into implementations and out to new physical domains. Instead of only analyzing standards, researchers attacked real silicon and firmware — "FirmXRay" (CCS 2020) mined BLE bugs from bare-metal firmware, "FirmWire" (NDSS 2022) made cellular baseband firmware transparently analyzable, and "Noncompliance as Deviant Behavior" (CCS 2021) automatically caught devices that deviate from the LTE spec. Attacks also moved past traditional protocols to satellites and sensing: "A Tale of Sea and Sky" (S&P 2020) and "Space Odyssey" (S&P 2023) opened up maritime VSAT and satellite security, while "mmSpy" (S&P 2022) and "IRShield" (S&P 2022) showed how mmWave and physical-layer sensing can both attack and defend privacy. Practical eavesdropping landed too, with "Call Me Maybe" (USENIX 2020) decrypting real VoLTE calls via key reuse.

Where the area stands now is a balance between offense, deployment-grade realism, and defense. GPS work matured from lab spoofing to real-world demonstrations, as in "An Experimental Study of GPS Spoofing and Takeover Attacks on UAVs" (USENIX 2022), and 5G research began proposing fixes rather than only breaks, e.g. "Privacy-Preserving and Standard-Compatible AKA Protocol for 5G" (USENIX 2021). The frontier has also absorbed machine learning, with "Robust Adversarial Attacks Against DNN-Based Wireless Communication Systems" (CCS 2021), and countermeasures like "IRShield" signal a growing emphasis on protecting users against the very physical-layer leakage earlier work exposed. Across a decade and four top venues, the arc runs from formally breaking standards, to exploiting them over the air, to digging into firmware and silicon, to securing an ever-widening set of RF systems from cellular to satellites.
